newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algerian moderate Islamist speaks of poll killings.
newsitem.headline: Algerian moderate Islamist speaks of poll killings.

text.p: Algeria's leading moderate Islamist leader said on Friday a "real massacre" took place in the western Algerian city of Tlemsan in violence related to Thursday's general election.
"A real massacre took place in which there were (people) killed and wounded in Boudgham district," Mahfoud Nahnah told a news conference shortly after midnight at his party's headquarters.
"It is related to the elections," he added, refusing to be drawn to give any further details.
There was no immediate word on the reported incident from the authorities.
The statement by the Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS) leader was the first report of a major outbreak of violence during the parliamentary election which is opposed by radical Islamist rebels.
MPS sources said a bomb wrecked a car carrying local election observers near the central city of Djelfa on Thursday and two monitors were seriously wounded in the blast. MPS is contesting the poll.

More than 10.6 million Algerians -- or 66.30 percent of eligible voters -- inside Algeria voted in Thursday's election, the first in five years of bloodshed. Hundreds of thousands of Algerians voted abroad.

The election was the first since Moslem fundamentalists dominated a December 1991 poll. The military-backed authorities cancelled that election in January 1992 and shortly afterwards the country plunged into violence in which an estimated 60,000 people died.
The pro-government National Democratic Rally (RND) party said on Friday it was doing well as election results began to trickle in.
But it did not give any figures and officials were not releasing any early results.
Algiers state radio said Interior Minister Mustapha Benmansour would declare the final results "after" 11 a.m. (1000 GMT) on Friday.
"We are in a very respectable position," RND spokesman Hamraoui Habib Chawki told Reuters. "The results that we have from the various provinces put the party constantly in the top three positions."
But Chawki hinted that the party would not be able to gain an absolute majority at the 380-seat National Assembly, the lower house.
"From now on there will not be any single dominant force. This will help the development of democracy and diversify the lower house," he said.
A new proportional representation law makes it very difficult for a single party to gain an absolute majority.

Security was tight at polling stations as voters cast ballots between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. (0700 GMT and 1900 GMT) on Thursday to choose from more than 7,000 candidates representing 39 political parties.
A wave of bombings in Algiers by suspected Moslem rebels killed 22 people in the run-up to the election.
The U.S. State Department praised the voters for turning out in force saying they had shown "courage because they have been subjected to the most vicious case of terrorism over many, many years".
"I voted for peace," Ahmed Yanaguen, 58, said after he and his wife, wearing a black veil, were the first to vote at El- Warda school in the capital's Telemly neighbourhood.
The government of President Liamine Zeroual says the poll is a key step towards ending the civil strife.

Sceptics in the Algerian capital doubt the level of violence would soon drop because the new assembly will be deprived of any real power and will not be able to push for dialogue with radical Islamists.

The RND's main competitors include Nahnah's Islam-oriented MPS, the Socialist Forces Front (FFS) of secularist opposition leader Hocine Ait Ahmed and the Rally for Culture and Democracy of anti-Islamist Said Saadi.
Several party leaders complained of irregularities at the election but Interior Minister Benmansour dismissed the complaints as "political competition".
"Algeria does not allow itself to permit -- even by local authorities -- such irregularities," he said.
